tagline: River villages and a former turnpike lead into the Green Mountains.
intro: The Mad River Byway combines a valley drive with a climb into the Green Mountains. The Mad River Valley Chamber of Commerce describes a 36.5-mile scenic route on Routes 2, 100, 100B and 17, much of it beside the Green Mountain National Forest. It places the byway among Vermont roads recognized for cultural, historic, natural, recreational and scenic qualities, highlighting covered bridges and waterfalls. At Moretown, farm fields flank the river beneath forested hills; the Route 17 climb to Appalachian Gap has sustained pitches above 15 percent.

These roads developed along different paths. An early road between Granville and Waitsfield followed the Mad River through Warren’s Main Street. West of the valley, the McCullough Turnpike was chartered in 1933 but proved unprofitable. The state took over part in 1936 and the remainder to Waitsfield in 1956; Route 17 was extended across the mountains in 1965.

Start at Middlesex and follow Route 100B southwest to Moretown, then Route 100 toward Waitsfield. At Waitsfield, the Route 17 branch passes Mad River Glen toward Appalachian Gap. Return to Route 100 for Warren and Granville Gulf, where the headwaters divide between the north-flowing Mad River and the south-flowing White River system.

moments.title: Great Eddy Covered Bridge
moments.text: The Great Eddy Covered Bridge spans the Mad River just east of central Waitsfield. A bridge already crossed here in 1797, before the Richardson family laid out the present village center in 1817. Built in 1833, its 105-foot span uses Burr trusses, each incorporating a laminated arch. The walkway beneath the extended metal roof came later, in 1940. During Hurricane Irene in 2011, floodwater rose until no clearance remained beneath the bridge. The bridge survived while nearby buildings were lifted from their foundations. After another closure for repairs in 2015, it reopened in November 2016.

moments.title: Mad River Glen
moments.text: Mad River Glen’s Single Chair carries one skier at a time. The lift first operated in 1948, when five trails and a small base lodge were also completed. Founder Roland Palmedo wanted a ski area for dedicated skiers with few commercial amenities. In 1995, owner Betsy Pratt sold the area to skiers who formed a cooperative to own and manage it. Shareholders elect trustees to oversee the business, while the mountain retains narrow trails and limited grooming. The ski area became a National Register historic district in 2012, recognizing the place that grew from that single-chair beginning.

moments.title: Granville
moments.text: At Granville Gulf, the road crosses a divide between two river systems. The Mad River begins north of the height of land and drains toward the Winooski River and Lake Champlain. Southward, Alder Meadow Brook drains into the White River, then the Connecticut River and Long Island Sound. Route 100 runs through the gulf north of Granville’s village. The surrounding reservation includes Moss Glen Falls, where Deer Hollow Brook joins the southward drainage. Beyond the gulf, Granville lies between Braintree Ridge to the east and the main crest of the Green Mountains to the west.
